content.narrative_summary: The 2025 ACC/AHA/HRS/ISACHD/SCAI Guideline for the Management of Adults With Congenital Heart Disease provides recommendations to guide clinicians on the evaluation and treatment of adult patients with congenital heart disease, replacing the 2018 AHA/ACC Guideline. A comprehensive literature search of publications from 2017 to 2024 (with selected older sources) was conducted using MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane Library, AHRQ, and CINAHL. Recommendations from the 2018 guideline have been updated with new evidence to guide clinical practice.

content.title: What Is New
content.narrative_summary: Table 1 highlights new and/or substantially revised practice-changing recommendations since the last iteration of the guideline; it is not a comprehensive list of all updates. Some of these recommendations have corresponding footnotes not included in this table.

rows.recommendation: Patients in adult congenital heart disease (ACHD) anatomic-physiological (AP) class IA should have at least 1 evaluation by an ACHD cardiologist to develop a plan of care.

In patients with ACHD AP classifications IC-D, IIB-D, and IIIA-D who undergo noncardiac procedures, postprocedural care should involve collaboration with an ACHD cardiologist to incorporate expert opinion, provide guideline-based medical therapy (GDMT), and improve outcomes.

In patients with ACHD AP classifications IC-D, IIC-D, and IIIA-D, anesthesia for noncardiac procedures should be administered by, or in collaboration or consultation with, an anesthesiologist with ACHD expertise to reduce the likelihood of perioperative complications.

In patients with ACHD who undergo invasive cardiac procedures, preprocedural involvement of an ACHD cardiologist is recommended to risk-stratify the patient, determine appropriate procedure location, guide periprocedural planning and support, and assist in preprocedural clinical optimization to improve outcomes.

In patients with ACHD undergoing invasive cardiac procedures, postprocedural care should involve collaboration with an ACHD cardiologist to incorporate expert opinion, provide guideline-based therapy, and improve outcomes.

In patients with ACHD AP classifications IC-D, IIA-D, and IIIA-D, anesthesia for invasive cardiac procedures should be administered by, or in collaboration or consultation with, an anesthesiologist who has congenital heart disease expertise to reduce the likelihood of perioperative complications.

In patients with ACHD who undergo invasive cardiac procedures for acquired cardiovascular disease, it can be beneficial for operators with expertise in procedural treatment of acquired disease to collaborate with ACHD experts.

In adults with congenital heart disease and a family history of congenital heart disease or clinical features associated with a genetic syndrome, referral for genetic evaluation is reasonable to guide management.

For patients with ACHD who are considering assisted reproductive technology, discussions involving an ACHD cardiologist can be beneficial to increase patients’ knowledge about their options and the associated risks.
Routine cesarean delivery has no benefit and may cause harm in pregnant patients with ACHD in the absence of an obstetric indication or high-risk cardiac condition.

In patients with ACHD, participation in competitive sports is reasonable following a comprehensive evaluation by an ACHD specialist that incorporates functional status and individualized assessment of risks and benefits.

Adults with an unrepaired atrial septal defect (ASD) and pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) should undergo risk assessment and management in consultation with pulmonary hypertension specialists to improve outcomes.

rows.recommendation: In adults with an isolated unrepaired secundum ASD, transcatheter closure is usually preferred to surgical repair to reduce length of stay and recovery time.
In adults with an unrepaired ASD and evidence of (or strong suspicion for) paradoxical embolism, ASD closure is recommended to prevent recurrent embolism.

In adults with an unrepaired ASD, significant left-to-right shunt (Qp:Qs ≥1.5), right ventricular (RV) dilation, PAH (PVR 5–8 Wood units), and without significant left ventricular (LV) disease, closure can be beneficial if PVR <5 Wood units can be achieved with targeted PAH therapy, to improve medium-term functional status.
Patients with an unrepaired ventricular septal defect (VSD) should be assessed for the presence of PAH to guide decisions about medical therapy and repair.

In adults with a perimembranous VSD being considered for repair, evaluation to exclude right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) obstruction or double-chambered right ventricle (DCRV) is recommended to improve management planning.
Adults with a VSD (repaired or unrepaired) and PAH should be followed by specialists with expertise in ACHD and pulmonary hypertension to reduce morbidity and mortality.
No Benefit: In adults with a VSD, Qp:Qs <1.5, and no other indications, closure should not be performed to avoid unnecessary perioperative risks.

In adults with an unrepaired AVSD or those with residual shunts after previous repair, significant left-to-right shunt (Qp:Qs ≥1.5), and/or significant or progressive atrial/ventricular dilation with no PAH (PVR ≤2 Wood units), closure of the AVSD or residual shunt is recommended to improve functional class and clinical outcomes.
In adults with an AVSD (repaired or unrepaired) and PAH should be managed by pulmonary hypertension specialists and by clinicians with pulmonary hypertension expertise to improve outcomes.

In adults with repaired AVSD and LVOT obstruction with symptoms attributable to the obstruction, or LV systolic dysfunction (LV ejection fraction <50%), surgical repair is recommended to improve functional status and preserve ventricular function.

In adults with an unrepaired AVSD or those with residual shunts after previous repair, significant left-to-right shunt (Qp:Qs ≥1.5), and/or significant or progressive atrial/ ventricular dilation with no PAH (PVR ≤2 Wood units), closure of the AVSD or residual shunt is recommended to improve functional class and clinical outcomes.

For adults with anomalous pulmonary venous connections (APVCs) who do not have an indication for repair, routine cardiac imaging is recommended for serial evaluation of RV size and function and for assessment of pulmonary hypertension.

For adults with repaired APVCs and dyspnea on exertion and/or reduced functional capacity, cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) or computed tomography (CT) angiography is recommended to evaluate for venous obstruction or residual shunt.
No Benefit: For adults with APVCs who have a normal to mildly enlarged right ventricle and whose Qp:Qs is <1.5, surgical repair is not indicated, given the absence of data to support benefit.

rows.recommendation: In adults with unrepaired cor tritriatum sinister, transesophageal echocardiography and/or cross-sectional imaging can be useful to identify the size and location of the membrane orifice and to assess for the presence of associated congenital cardiac defects.
In asymptomatic adults with unrepaired cor tritriatum sinister and severe membrane obstruction, surgical resection can be useful to prevent the sequelae of left atrial hypertension.

In adults with unrepaired cor tritriatum sinister and atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter, prior stroke, or left atrial thrombus, chronic anticoagulation is recommended to prevent embolic stroke, whether or not conventional thromboembolic risk factors are present.
In adults with unrepaired cor tritriatum sinister and atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter, a rhythm control strategy can be beneficial to avoid clinical decompensation.

Adults with multiple left-sided obstructive lesions (Shone complex) and suspected pulmonary hypertension should undergo invasive hemodynamic assessment to identify and classify pulmonary hypertension.

Adults with a bicuspid aortic valve who have an aortic diameter >4 cm at the level of the sinuses or the ascending aorta, or who have risk factors for aortic dissection, should undergo lifelong surveillance for progression of thoracic aortic disease to improve early detection of aortic growth.

In adults with a congenitally abnormal aortic valve who meet indications for valve replacement, surgical and transcatheter options should be reviewed by heart valve and ACHD expert teams in a shared decision-making process to determine a management plan.
In adults with coarctation of the aorta who present with exertional symptoms, evaluation for coronary artery disease is reasonable to guide management.

In adults with Ebstein anomaly, an electrophysiological study is recommended for patients with symptomatic arrhythmia or asymptomatic ventricular preexcitation to assess for substrates for ablation, including multiple or high-risk accessory pathways.

In asymptomatic adults with moderate or severe valvular pulmonary stenosis and at least moderate tricuspid regurgitation or any RV dysfunction, pulmonary valve intervention is recommended to reduce pressure overload and improve valvular function.

In adults with moderate or greater pulmonary regurgitation resulting from treated isolated valvular pulmonary stenosis, CMR imaging is recommended to establish anatomy, quantify the degree of regurgitation, and measure RV volumes and systolic function.
In adults with RV dysfunction or symptoms attributed to DCRV, cardiac catheterization is reasonable to characterize anatomy and severity.
In adults with DCRV and moderate or greater RVOT obstruction, diagnostic assessment with CMR (or, if contraindicated, cardiac CT) can be beneficial to characterize the anatomy.
In adults with symptoms related to peripheral or branch PA stenosis, pulmonary branch balloon angioplasty and/or stent implantation is recommended to improve hemodynamics and symptoms.

In adults with repaired tetralogy of Fallot (TOF), echocardiography is recommended for assessment of pulmonary and tricuspid valve dysfunction, right atrial size, ventricular size and function, residual VSDs, and estimation of RV systolic pressure to characterize residual hemodynamic sequelae.

rows.recommendation: In adults with repaired TOF and native RVOT anatomy being considered for transcatheter pulmonary valve replacement, cardiac CT is recommended to determine anatomic suitability.

In adults with repaired TOF and appropriate implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) therapies for monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, adjunctive catheter ablation is reasonable to reduce ventricular tachyarrhythmia burden.

In adults with repaired TOF with moderate or greater pulmonary valve dysfunction and progressive ventricular systolic dysfunction, pulmonary valve replacement (surgical or transcatheter) is reasonable to preserve ventricular function.

In adults with a right ventricle-to-pulmonary artery (RV-to-PA) conduit being considered for transcatheter intervention, preprocedural coronary CT is reasonable to assess conduit calcification, anatomic characteristics, and coronary artery proximity to guide procedural planning.

For adults with an RV-to-PA conduit, severe stenosis and/or severe regurgitation, and symptoms or worsening functional capacity or a sustained arrhythmia, conduit intervention should be performed to improve cardiovascular status.
rows.supporting_text: 2018 Recommendation: COR 2a: RV-to-PA conduit intervention is reasonable for adults with an RV-to-PA conduit and moderate or greater PR or moderate or greater stenosis with reduced functional capacity or arrhythmia.

rows.recommendation: Adults with dextro-transposition of the great arteries (d-TGA) and atrial switch who present with progressive exercise intolerance or HF should undergo cardiopulmonary exercise testing to assess for potential intervention targets, including arrhythmia and desaturation.

Adults with d-TGA and atrial switch with progressive exercise intolerance, HF, pulmonary hypertension, worsening atrial or ventricular tachyarrhythmia, pathway obstruction, or baffle leak should undergo invasive hemodynamic assessment to identify targets for medical, percutaneous, or surgical intervention.
rows.supporting_text: 2018 Recommendation: COR 2a: Assessment for a communication through the interatrial baffle or venous stenosis is reasonable for adults with d-TGA with atrial switch, particularly if transvenous pacemaker/ICD implantation is considered or leads are already present.

rows.recommendation: Adults with d-TGA and atrial switch who require permanent pacemaker or an ICD should undergo preprocedural imaging, in addition to intraprocedural contrast venography, to detect baffle stenosis and residual baffle leaks.

For adults with d-TGA and atrial switch, biomarkers and validated disease-specific risk scores can be useful to identify patients at high risk for adverse cardiac events, prompting closer follow-up and referral to specialized HF transplant centers.

In adults with d-TGA and atrial switch with new or progressive symptoms of HF, it is reasonable to obtain a resting electrocardiogram and outpatient ambulatory rhythm monitoring, to ensure timely diagnosis and treatment of tachyarrhythmia or bradyarrhythmia.
rows.supporting_text: 2018 Recommendation: COR 1: Ambulatory monitoring for bradycardia or sinus node dysfunction is recommended for adults with d-TGA with atrial switch, especially if treated with beta blockers or other rate-slowing agents.

rows.recommendation: Adults with d-TGA and atrial switch who have symptoms attributable to a baffle leak should undergo closure of the leak to improve symptoms and quality of life.

In adults with d-TGA and atrial switch who have symptoms attributable to systemic or pulmonary venous pathway stenosis or liver congestion, intervention to relieve the stenosis is indicated to improve symptoms and prognosis.

Adults with d-TGA and atrial switch who have worsening symptoms of exercise intolerance, HF, or arrhythmia refractory to treatment should be referred to a HF program for assessment for mechanical support and transplantation in consultation with an ACHD cardiologist, to improve quality of life and prolong survival.
In adults with d-TGA and atrial switch who have sustained intra-atrial reentrant arrhythmias or atrial fibrillation, oral anticoagulation can be useful to prevent embolic events.
rows.supporting_text: 2018 Recommendation: COR 1: GDMT with appropriate attention to the need for anticoagulation is recommended to promptly restore sinus rhythm for adults with d-TGA with atrial switch repair presenting with atrial arrhythmia.

rows.recommendation: Adults with d-TGA and atrial switch who require transvenous lead placement can benefit from catheter-based interventions to address residual baffle leaks or obstruction before lead placement, to reduce the risk for systemic thromboembolism and/or future baffle occlusion.

In adults with an arterial switch operation and symptoms concerning for myocardial ischemia, coronary evaluation with coronary angiography, cross-sectional imaging, and/or functional coronary assessment for an anatomic etiology should be performed.
In adults with an arterial switch operation and evidence of myocardial ischemia, coronary revascularization should be performed to reduce symptoms and improve outcomes.

In asymptomatic adults with an arterial switch operation who have moderate or greater supravalvar or branch PA stenosis—in addition to RV hypertension, RV dysfunction, progressive tricuspid regurgitation, and/or objective decline in exercise capacity—intervention can be useful to relieve obstruction.

In adults with congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries (CCTGA), periodic transthoracic echocardiography is recommended to assess chamber function, systemic tricuspid valve function, and associated anatomic lesions such as septal defects and LVOT stenosis.
In adults with CCTGA without symptoms, periodic ambulatory rhythm monitoring is reasonable to screen for high-grade atrioventricular block.
In symptomatic adults with CCTGA and high-grade atrioventricular block, physiological pacing (CRT or conduction system pacing) is reasonable to relieve symptoms.

In adults with Fontan circulation and evidence of progressive Fontan circulatory failure, formal evaluation by a HF/transplant cardiologist with experience in heart transplantation in the adult Fontan population is recommended.

In adults with Fontan circulation, imaging and laboratory evaluation of the liver should be performed at least annually to screen for hepatocellular carcinoma and for evidence of progressive Fontan-associated liver disease.

In adults with Fontan circulation and new or progressive symptoms, hypoxemia, declining functional status, or evidence of progressive or new-onset noncardiac organ dysfunction, hemodynamic evaluation with cardiac catheterization is recommended to guide therapy.

In adults with Fontan circulation and newly progressive or severe hypoxemia or hypotension, evaluation with advanced cardiac imaging (CMR, CT, transesophageal echocardiography) is recommended to rule out thrombus or emboli in the Fontan or pulmonary vasculature.

In adults with Fontan circulation undergoing CT angiography to rule out thrombus or emboli in the Fontan or pulmonary vasculature, imaging should be performed using protocols to avoid false-negative or false-positive results.

In adults with Fontan circulation, consultation by a hepatologist, in collaboration with an ACHD cardiologist, is reasonable to facilitate interpretation of hepatic testing, diagnose and treat complications related to portal hypertension, and participate in timing and management decisions specific to organ transplantation.
In adults with Fontan circulation, liver biopsy can be helpful to delineate the degree of hepatic fibrosis or cirrhosis before consideration of transplantation.

In adults with Fontan circulation and sinus node dysfunction requiring pacemaker placement, atrial-based pacing with programming to minimize ventricular pacing is recommended to improve patient symptoms and to avoid pacing-induced cardiomyopathy.

rows.recommendation: In adults with Fontan circulation with new-onset atrial flutter or atrial fibrillation, timely cardioversion (pharmacological or electrical) is recommended to prevent clinical decompensation.

Adults with Fontan circulation referred for cardiac transplantation should undergo pretransplantation review by a committee with broad multidisciplinary representation to improve patient selection and posttransplant outcomes.

In adults with Fontan circulation and atrioventricular block whose burden of ventricular pacing is likely to be high (ie, >40%), apical site pacing is preferred over nonapical sites to improve transplant-free survival.
In adults with Fontan circulation, formal exercise programs and/or cardiac rehabilitation (appropriate to the patient's ability) can be beneficial in improving functional capacity.

In adults with Fontan circulation and hemodynamically significant stenosis of the Fontan or PAs, catheter-based stenting of the stenosis to reduce Fontan pressure and improve flow is reasonable to improve hemodynamics.

In symptomatic adults with Fontan circulation, or those with evidence of systemic ventricular volume overload, closure of aortopulmonary collaterals to improve symptoms and reduce the likelihood of pathologic ventricular remodeling can be useful.
In adults with Fontan circulation, annual laboratory evaluation is recommended to assess for evidence of organ-system dysfunction or hematologic abnormality.
rows.supporting_text: COR 2a: In adults after Fontan palliation, it is reasonable to perform biochemical and hematological testing on an annual basis, especially for liver and renal function.

rows.recommendation: In adults with Fontan circulation and the absence of high-risk features (history of thromboembolism, sustained atrial flutter/fibrillation, or atriopulmonary Fontan) or bleeding contraindications, treatment with either aspirin or anticoagulation is recommended to reduce the probability of thromboembolic disease.
rows.supporting_text: COR 2b: Antiplatelet therapy or anticoagulation with a vitamin K antagonist may be considered in adults after Fontan palliation without known or suspected thrombus, thromboembolic events, or prior arrhythmia.

rows.recommendation: Adults with Eisenmenger syndrome should be advised against pregnancy to decrease the risk associated with excess maternal morbidity and mortality.

In adults with Eisenmenger syndrome and an LV ejection fraction >40% who are symptomatic or have reduced exercise capacity, initial monotherapy with PAH-directed therapy is recommended to improve symptoms, hemodynamics and overall survival.
rows.supporting_text: COR 2a: Bosentan is a reasonable therapy to treat symptomatic adults with Eisenmenger syndrome with 1 of the following: shunts other than ASD/VSD (eg, PDA, aortopulmonary window), or complex congenital heart lesions or Down syndrome.

rows.recommendation: In adults with Eisenmenger syndrome and an LV ejection fraction >40% who are symptomatic or have reduced exercise capacity, initial monotherapy with PAH-directed therapy is recommended to improve symptoms, hemodynamics, and overall survival.
rows.supporting_text: COR 2a: It is reasonable to use phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE-5) inhibitors (eg, sildenafil, tadalafil) to treat symptomatic adults with Eisenmenger syndrome with ASD, VSD, or great artery shunt.

rows.recommendation: In adults with Eisenmenger syndrome and an LV ejection fraction >40% who remain symptomatic or have worsening exercise capacity on a single PAH therapy, dual combination therapy with an endothelin receptor antagonist and a PDE-5 inhibitor is recommended to improve symptoms, hemodynamics, and overall survival.
rows.supporting_text: COR 2a: In symptomatic adults with Eisenmenger syndrome, bosentan and PDE-5 inhibitors are reasonable in combination if symptomatic improvement does not occur with either medication alone.

rows.recommendation: In adults with Eisenmenger syndrome who present with atrial arrhythmias, prompt restoration and maintenance of sinus rhythm is recommended to avoid hemodynamic deterioration.
In adults with Eisenmenger syndrome, a regular exercise program in combination with directed PAH therapy can be effective in improving exercise capacity.
Adults with Eisenmenger syndrome should not be routinely prescribed oral anticoagulation given the high bleeding risk and lack of long-term survival benefit.

content.narrative_summary: This page outlines the intended use of ACC/AHA clinical practice guidelines, emphasizing applicability to patients with or at risk of cardiovascular disease and noting they are not replacements for clinical judgment. It describes the necessity of shared decision-making for guideline implementation. The Methodology and Modernization section details the ACC/AHA Joint Committee’s continuous review and modular “knowledge chunk” format to enhance user-friendliness and evidence dissemination. The writing committee selection process aims for broad expertise and diversity. Policies on managing relationships with industry and other entities to avoid bias are summarized. Finally, the evidence review process is described, noting reliance on evidence-based methodologies, systematic reviews, and commissioning of independent committees for key clinical questions.

content.narrative_summary: This page provides the introduction to the 2025 ACC/AHA guideline for adults with congenital heart disease. It defines guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) encompassing clinical evaluation, diagnostic testing, and pharmacological and procedural treatments, limited to US-approved drugs, devices, and treatments. Section 1.1 describes the evidence review process—English-language studies indexed in MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane Library, and other databases from May to September 2024, with additional studies through July 2025—and summarizes the Evidence Table. Section 1.2 outlines the composition of the multidisciplinary writing committee, including adult and pediatric ACHD cardiologists, surgeons, electrophysiologists, nurses, and a patient advocate representing AHA, ACC, HRS, ISACHD, and SCAI. Section 1.3 details the peer review and approval process by the ACC, AHA, HRS, ISACHD, and SCAI, with disclosures published. Section 1.4 defines the scope of the guideline as a full revision of the 2018 guideline, incorporating new data on structural cardiac abnormalities, excluding inherited disorders (eg, Marfan syndrome, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy), anatomic variants (eg, patent foramen ovale), and pediatric (<18 years) congenital heart disease, and focusing on adult congenital valve disease distinct from acquired valve disease.

section_headings: 3.1.1. Transition Education and Transfer of Care
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis identifies key challenges in transition education for congenital heart disease, including lack of universal patient identification in electronic medical record systems, absence of standardized, developmentally and educationally appropriate materials tailored to patients’ age, sex, gender, and learning ability, inadequate resources and qualified personnel to administer education, and lack of methodology for measuring transition success. It emphasizes that unsuccessful transfer of care from pediatric to adult congenital heart disease (ACHD) providers may lead to gaps in care delivery and unexpected morbidity.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Transition Education and Transfer of Care

rows.recommendation: All patients with congenital heart disease should receive structured, patient-centered transition education that is age-, sex-, gender-, and developmentally appropriate to improve knowledge (LOE A) and reduce loss to care (LOE B-NR).
Congenital heart disease programs and clinicians should have transfer-of-care policies and procedures to ensure effective handoffs of patients from a pediatric to an ACHD cardiologist.

content.narrative_summary: The Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education and the American Boards of Internal Medicine and Pediatrics established formal training and board certification for ACHD cardiologists, improving adult outcomes when care is delivered by organized, multidisciplinary ACHD programs. Table 7 lists recommended program personnel and services. While patients with ACHD may be followed by individual cardiologists, complex diagnoses should prompt referral to specialized multidisciplinary care, balancing access constraints (geography, insurance, socioeconomic factors). Indications for program referral include worsening AP class, advanced CT/CMR imaging, heart failure, transplant evaluation/listing, diagnostic/interventional catheterization, electrophysiology procedures, cardiothoracic surgery, pregnancy management, and high-risk noncardiac surgery. After initial consultation and AP class confirmation, patients with mild disease (class IA) may continue with general cardiologists but require awareness of possible complications. The predominant entry to ACHD care is transfer from pediatric providers; many patients are lost to care before or after transfer, and their subsequent care pathways often remain unknown.

content.title: 3.2. Expertise for Noncardiac Surgery
content.narrative_summary: Patients with ACHD have increased operative risk for noncardiac surgery. Recommendations emphasize preprocedural involvement of an ACHD cardiologist, postoperative collaboration with an ACHD cardiologist, and anesthesia management by an ACHD‐expert anesthesiologist. Supporting text reviews higher risk influenced by congenital lesion type, urgency, physiology, and specialized resource needs, and the importance of individualized pre-, intra-, and postoperative planning and management.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Expertise for Noncardiac Surgery

rows.recommendation: In patients with ACHD being considered for noncardiac procedures, preprocedural involvement of an ACHD cardiologist is recommended to risk-stratify the patient, determine appropriate procedure location, guide periprocedural planning and support, and assist in preprocedural clinical optimization to improve outcomes.1,2

In patients with ACHD AP classifications IC-D, IIB-D, and IIIA-D who undergo noncardiac procedures, postprocedural care should involve collaboration with an ACHD cardiologist to incorporate expert opinion, provide guideline-based therapy, and improve outcomes.1-3

In patients with ACHD AP classifications IC-D, IIC-D, and IIIA-D, anesthesia for noncardiac procedures should be administered by, or in collaboration or consultation with, an anesthesiologist with ACHD expertise to reduce the likelihood of perioperative complications.4-6

For adults with congenital heart disease, neuropsychological testing may be considered to guide therapies that enhance academic, behavioral, psychosocial, and adaptive functioning.

content.title: Expertise for Cardiac Surgery and Invasive Cardiac Procedures
section_headings: 3.4. Expertise for Cardiac Surgery and Invasive Cardiac Procedures
content.narrative_summary: Patients with adult congenital heart disease (ACHD) undergoing invasive cardiac procedures require specialized multidisciplinary care. Preprocedural, intraprocedural, and postprocedural management should involve an ACHD cardiologist to guide risk stratification, planning, and optimization, and an anesthesiologist with congenital heart disease expertise to reduce perioperative complications. Expertise in ACHD spans cardiology, congenital heart surgery, electrophysiology, and anesthesia, often gained through dedicated fellowship training or focused clinical practice. Patients with complex physiology (e.g., single ventricle palliation, shunt-related cyanosis) pose unique challenges and benefit from specialized practitioners and guideline-based therapy. ACHD patients also have complex anatomy and physiology that increase the technical and medical risks of invasive cardiac procedures.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Expertise for Cardiac Surgery and Invasive Cardiac Procedures

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with ACHD who undergo invasive cardiac procedures, preprocedural involvement of an ACHD cardiologist is recommended to risk‐stratify the patient, determine appropriate procedure location, guide periprocedural planning and support, and assist in preprocedural clinical optimization to improve outcomes.1-3

2. In patients with ACHD, invasive cardiac procedures involving congenital lesions should be performed by operators with expertise in congenital heart disease procedures to ensure appropriate peri‐procedural care.4,5

3. In patients with ACHD undergoing invasive cardiac procedures, post‐procedural care should involve collaboration with an ACHD cardiologist to incorporate expert opinion, provide guideline‐based therapy, and improve outcomes.1,3,4

4. In patients with ACHD AP classifications IC-D, IIA-D, and IIIA-D, anesthesia for invasive cardiac procedures should be administered by, or in collaboration or consultation with, an anesthesiologist who has congenital heart disease expertise to reduce the likelihood of perioperative complications.2,3,6,7

5. In patients with ACHD who undergo invasive cardiac procedures for acquired cardiovascular disease, it can be beneficial for operators with expertise in procedural treatment of acquired disease to collaborate with ACHD experts.8-10

continuity.reason: Page narrative and synopsis sections end mid-sentence, indicating continuation on the next page.

content.narrative_summary: The page continues the discussion of peri-procedural management in adult congenital heart disease (ACHD), emphasizing that collaboration with ACHD-experienced surgeons, interventional cardiologists, and electrophysiologists optimizes planning and reduces procedural risk. Specialized ACHD practitioners improve postprocedural follow-up and outcomes, while non-specialized care is associated with higher adverse event rates. Operators must account for complex aortopulmonary sequelae, unique physiology, anesthetic effects, and ventilation strategies during invasive procedures. Although ACHD-specific anesthesia training is limited, advanced pediatric or adult congenital cardiac anesthesiology experience, mentoring, and practice improve safety. As ACHD patients age, they face acquired cardiovascular diseases, and co-surgeon or multidisciplinary care models involving congenital and acquired disease experts enhance outcomes.

Referenced studies that support recommendations are summarized in the Evidence Table.

rows.recommendation: 1. Patients with ACHD and cyanosis should receive annual screening for and treatment of iron deficiency to improve exercise capacity and functional status.
2. In patients with ACHD and cyanosis who present with persistent, new, or worsening neurologic deficits, urgent brain imaging to exclude cerebral abscess or stroke should be performed.

3. In patients with ACHD and cyanosis who present with symptoms of hyperviscosity, rehydration with oral or intravenous fluids should be performed to improve symptoms and reduce the risk for vascular complications.

4. Pregnant patients with ACHD and cyanosis should be closely followed for the entire duration of the pregnancy by a multidisciplinary cardio-obstetrics team of experts in maternal-fetal medicine, ACHD, and obstetric anesthesia to reduce the risk for pregnancy-related cardiovascular and obstetric complications.

5. Patients with ACHD and cyanosis who are of childbearing age should receive comprehensive family planning consultation, including recommendations on safe and reliable contraceptive methods, from a multidisciplinary team of experts in family planning and ACHD.
6. In patients with ACHD and cyanosis who experience recurrent unexplained hypertension or tachycardia, evaluation to detect pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas is reasonable.

content.title: 2025 ACHD Guideline
content.narrative_summary: Continuing a list of management considerations for patients with ACHD and cyanosis: pregnancy-related cardiovascular, obstetric, and neonatal risks increase with disease complexity; estrogen-containing contraceptives raise thrombosis risk and should be avoided in cyanotic patients (5). Pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas occur more frequently in ACHD with cyanosis; screen using plasma and urinary fractionated metanephrines (6). Hyperuricemia and gout evaluation are common in cyanotic ACHD (7). Cyanotic patients have reduced exercise capacity; supplemental oxygen improves capacity (8). Phlebotomy (250–500 mL) may relieve hyperviscosity symptoms after hydration and iron correction, and for preoperative autologous transfusion if hematocrit >65% (9). Prophylactic phlebotomy is not recommended due to worsened iron deficiency and stroke risk and transient hematocrit effect (10). Synopsis: Heart failure in ACHD is a significant source of morbidity and mortality with high SCD risk; despite data on GDMT, CRT, mechanical support, and transplantation, randomized trials exclude ACHD patients and anatomy varies widely, limiting guideline recommendations.

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with ACHD and heart failure symptoms who have systemic left ventricular (LV) dysfunction and biventricular circulation, and who otherwise meet accepted criteria for cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT), use of CRT is reasonable to improve heart failure symptoms.1–4

2. In patients with ACHD and heart failure symptoms who have systemic LV systolic dysfunction and biventricular circulation, use of GDMT for heart failure is reasonable to improve heart failure symptoms.2,5–7

3. In patients with ACHD and heart failure symptoms who have systemic LV dysfunction and biventricular circulation, who otherwise meet accepted criteria, use of a primary-prevention implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) is reasonable to prevent sudden cardiac death (SCD).8,9

content.narrative_summary: The page continues discussion of advanced heart failure therapies in adults with congenital heart disease (ACHD), noting that anatomic and physiologic variability in ACHD alters benefits and harms of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) and device therapy compared with non-ACHD populations. It summarizes supportive evidence for three recommendation areas: 1) cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) improves ventricular activation and clinical outcomes in ACHD with systemic left ventricles and similar benefits in observational studies of ACHD; 2) GDMT in ACHD with systemic left ventricular systolic dysfunction shows retrospective improvements in ejection fraction, symptoms, and biomarker outcomes, and newer therapies such as ARNI and SGLT2 inhibitors appear safe; and 3) sudden cardiac death (SCD) risk in ACHD is elevated (25% of congenital heart disease mortality), with registry-derived risk models for Ebstein anomaly, Fontan physiology, and systemic right ventricles unvalidated, and no randomized trials for primary-prevention ICDs in ACHD, though data from noncongenital populations support ICD benefit in systemic left ventricular morphology, with a high inappropriate shock rate in tetralogy of Fallot.

content.title: 3.6.2. Heart Transplantation and MCS
content.narrative_summary: The narrative discusses long-term morbidity and reduced survival in adults with ACHD, highlighting heart failure as a leading cause of death and increased risk from prior transfusions and homografts. It notes benefits of the revised organ allocation system in reducing waitlist times and improving outcomes, and describes the use of temporary and durable MCS devices for stabilization and as a bridge to transplant. Supportive text outlines reversible causes of heart failure, evaluation triggers, criteria for advanced heart failure therapies including transplantation, and center-specific thresholds for multiorgan transplantation.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Heart Transplantation and MCS

rows.recommendation: In patients with ACHD and heart failure, evaluation by specialists with medical and surgical experience in ACHD, as well as by specialists with expertise in advanced heart failure, is recommended to assess appropriateness for advanced heart failure therapies, such as heart transplantation or MCS.1,2

In patients with ACHD who are considered for heart transplantation, multiorgan transplantation (heart–lung,3 heart–kidney,4 or heart–liver5,6) is reasonable based on center-specific assessment of the degree of respective lung, kidney, or liver dysfunction.

In patients with ACHD and advanced heart failure that is refractory to optimal medical and device-based therapy, the use of durable MCS devices is reasonable to improve quality of life or as a bridge to transplantation.7–10

content.narrative_summary: Patients with congenital heart disease are exposed to low‐dose ionizing radiation from cardiac procedures, which increases cancer risk and should be minimized through judicious test selection and optimized imaging protocols. Cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) is a reliable, reproducible tool that provides prognostic and diagnostic information on functional capacity, guiding clinical decision‐making and long‐term monitoring. When CPET is not feasible or in patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension, a 6‐minute walk test offers an alternative assessment of symptom severity, functional capacity, and therapy response. Patients often underreport limitations, so serial exercise testing should be integrated into longitudinal follow‐up.

rows.recommendation: In patients with ACHD, CPET can be useful for establishing a baseline functional assessment, guiding clinical care, stratifying risk for major adverse cardiovascular events, and ongoing surveillance.

In patients with ACHD and established PAH, or in those unable to perform CPET yielding reliable diagnostic information, a 6-minute walk test can be useful to objectively assess symptom severity, functional capacity, and response to therapy.

content.title: 3.10.2. Physical Activity, Exercise, and Sports Participation
section_headings: 3.10.2. Physical Activity, Exercise, and Sports Participation
content.narrative_summary: Recent guidelines for adults with congenital heart disease (ACHD) have shifted focus from exercise restriction to promotion of regular, moderate physical activity and tailored sports participation. Documented benefits include improved functional capacity, vascular and autonomic function, and patient-reported outcomes. Specific recommendations on this page call for routine assessment and counseling on exercise intensity, prescription of exercise training and cardiac rehabilitation to enhance capacity, use of cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) to tailor activity guidance, and reasonable competitive sports participation after comprehensive specialist evaluation. Supporting evidence highlights enhanced exercise capacity, heart failure symptoms, and quality of life, while noting potential challenges in program adherence and the need for individualized risk–benefit assessments.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Physical Activity, Exercise, and Sports Participation

rows.recommendation: 1. Patients with ACHD should have their activity levels assessed at regular intervals to receive counseling about the types and intensity of exercise appropriate to their clinical status.
2. In patients with ACHD, exercise training and cardiac rehabilitation can be useful to increase exercise capacity.
3. In patients with ACHD, CPET can be useful to guide physical activity recommendations.

4. In patients with ACHD, participation in competitive sports is reasonable following a comprehensive evaluation by an ACHD specialist that incorporates functional status and individualized assessment of risks and benefits.

content.narrative_summary: This section defines congenital shunt lesions (ASD, VSD, AVSD, PDA, anomalous pulmonary venous return), describes left-to-right versus right-to-left flow dynamics and hemodynamic criteria for significance (Qp:Qs ≥1.5), and explains clinical implications including chamber enlargement and exercise-induced bidirectional flow. It introduces PAH in ACHD patients by definition (mean PA pressure >20 mm Hg, PVR >2 Wood units, wedge pressure ≤15 mm Hg), outlines four PAH-ACHD subtypes, and emphasizes the role of pulmonary hypertension specialist care. Considerations for shunt closure based on pulmonary vascular resistance and risk of irreversible disease are discussed, noting contraindications for closure in severe cases and the possibility of partial (“fenestrated”) closure.

content.title: 4.1.1. Atrial Septal Defect
content.narrative_summary: Discussion notes that repair outcomes are most robust in pretricuspid shunts when PVR drops to <5 Wood units after PAH therapy. The treat-and-repair approach requires expert ACHD and pulmonary hypertension care, postclosure hemodynamic assessment, and typically long-term PAH therapies. Further management recommendations are provided in the individual lesion sections.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Atrial Septal Defect – Diagnostic

rows.recommendation: In adults with an unrepaired ASD, CMR imaging, transesophageal echocardiography, or cardiac CT is recommended to define defect size, morphology, rim anatomy, and pulmonary venous connections.
Adults with an unrepaired ASD and PAH should undergo risk assessment and management in consultation with pulmonary hypertension specialists to improve outcomes.
Adults with an unrepaired ASD should be assessed for the presence of PAH to guide medical therapy and determine suitability for repair.
In adults with an unrepaired ASD, balloon test occlusion before closure may be reasonable to assess hemodynamic changes.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Atrial Septal Defect – Therapeutic

rows.recommendation: In adults with an unrepaired ASD, significant left-to-right shunt (Qp:Qs ≥1.5) and right ventricular (RV) dilation, in the absence of PAH (PVR ≤2 Wood units) or significant LV disease,* ASD closure is recommended to improve functional class and clinical outcomes.
In adults with an isolated unrepaired secundum ASD, transcatheter closure is usually preferred to surgical repair to reduce length of stay and recovery time.

3. Adults with a PDA should undergo assessment of LV function and left-sided chamber size with echocardiography and/or CMR imaging, to guide recommendations for treatment.
4. In adults with a PDA and PAH, balloon test occlusion of the PDA can be useful to facilitate accurate quantification of PVR and to identify patients who are candidates for closure.²

6. In adults with a PDA, left heart enlargement attributable to the PDA, a net left-to-right shunt, and PVR >2 but <5 Wood units, closure to eliminate the shunt is reasonable to improve clinical outcomes.⁶–⁸

8. In asymptomatic adults with a PDA, no evidence of left atrial or LV enlargement, and no prior history of endarteritis, closure has no benefit.
9. In adults with a PDA and Eisenmenger syndrome or PVR >10 Wood units, closure to eliminate the shunt should not be performed to avoid additional morbidity or mortality risk.

content.title: 4.2.4. Congenital Diseases of the Aortic Valve
section_headings: 4.2.4. Congenital Diseases of the Aortic Valve
content.narrative_summary: Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) is the most common congenital cardiac abnormality, with an estimated prevalence of 4.6 per 1,000 live births and male predominance. It may occur in isolation or with other congenital lesions (eg, coarctation of the aorta [COA], truncus arteriosus, hypoplastic left heart syndrome, Turner syndrome, Shone complex). Early adverse left ventricular remodeling is detected by echocardiography and biomarkers (eg, NT-proBNP), and suggested imaging intervals for asymptomatic patients are provided in Table 22. While standard valve replacement indications apply, lifelong management of young adults requires individualized planning considering anatomy, lifestyle, and possible minimally invasive or transcatheter approaches. Supportive text highlights that COA occurs in 4%–10% of BAV cases, thoracic aortic disease prevalence may reach 30%–40% in referral cohorts, and retrospective data show low incidences of aortic dissection (≈1%) and ascending aortic replacement (1%–3%) in this population, with details continuing on the next page.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Congenital Diseases of the Aortic Valve

rows.recommendation: 1. Adults with a BAV should be screened for the presence of COA and aortic aneurysm to obtain early diagnosis and determine a management plan.

2. Adults with a BAV who have an aortic diameter >4 cm at the level of the sinuses or the ascending aorta, or who have risk factors for aortic dissection,* should undergo lifelong surveillance for progression of thoracic aortic disease to improve early detection of aortic growth.

3. In first-degree relatives of adults with a BAV, 1-time echocardiographic screening for the presence of a congenitally abnormal aortic valve or aortic aneurysm is reasonable to obtain early diagnosis.

4. In adults with a congenitally abnormal aortic valve who meet indication for valve replacement, surgical and transcatheter options should be reviewed by heart valve and ACHD expert teams in a shared decision-making process to determine a management plan.

5. In young adults with congenital aortic valve stenosis, a noncalcified valve with no more than mild aortic regurgitation, and an indication for intervention, balloon valvuloplasty may be reasonable to delay the need for aortic valve surgery.

content.title: 4.2.5. Supravalvar Aortic Stenosis
content.narrative_summary: The page defines supravalvar aortic stenosis as occurring distal to the coronary orifices at the sinotubular junction, in forms ranging from discrete, hourglass narrowings to diffuse, long-segment stenoses involving the ascending aorta and brachiocephalic vessels. It notes associations with Williams syndrome, homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, and nonsyndromic elastin arteriopathy. Adults with supravalvar aortic stenosis should undergo detailed baseline imaging of aortic anatomy, and those with Williams syndrome should have baseline coronary evaluation to assess for ostial stenosis and sudden cardiac death risk. Symptomatic patients or those with LV systolic dysfunction should be referred for surgical repair, with coronary revascularization recommended for ischemic symptoms. Supportive text discusses the utility and limitations of transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography, and the role of cross-sectional imaging (CMR, MR angiography, CT angiography) before and after repair. It emphasizes the increased coronary risk in Williams syndrome, the need for baseline coronary screening if not previously performed, and consideration of screening in nonsyndromic elastin arteriopathy given ELN gene abnormalities.

rows.recommendation: 1. In adults with suspected supravalvar aortic stenosis or with Williams syndrome, baseline aortic imaging is recommended to define the anatomy and severity of supravalvar aortic stenosis.¹,²
2. In adults with Williams syndrome and supravalvar aortic stenosis, baseline coronary imaging is recommended to evaluate for abnormalities such as coronary ostial stenosis.²–⁴

3. In adults with supravalvar aortic stenosis who are symptomatic and/or have diminished LV systolic function due to stenosis, surgical repair is recommended to alleviate symptoms and preserve ventricular function.⁵,⁶

4. Adults with supravalvar aortic stenosis and coronary ostial stenosis with symptoms of ischemia should undergo coronary artery revascularization to alleviate symptoms and preserve ventricular function.⁷

5. In adults with asymptomatic severe supravalvar aortic stenosis, normal ventricular size and function, and a normal exercise stress test, surgical repair may be considered to avoid worsening of cardiac function and symptoms.

content.narrative_summary: The synopsis defines coarctation of the aorta (COA) as a lesion of the aortic isthmus often associated with arch hypoplasia and LVOT disease, resulting in LV pressure overload, remodeling (hypertrophy, fibrosis, impaired relaxation), endothelial dysfunction, and increased arterial stiffness. Chronic LV remodeling can lead to diastolic and systolic dysfunction, heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, atrial fibrillation, premature coronary artery disease, stroke, and other vascular complications. The supportive text emphasizes that patients with new or suspected COA require transthoracic echocardiography and cross-sectional imaging (CMR/CT angiography) to characterize lesion severity, anatomy, and intracardiac findings for optimal therapy. In repaired COA, long-term imaging surveillance is needed to detect re-coarctation, wall injury, aneurysms/pseudoaneurysms, and aortic dissection, enabling timely intervention to reduce mortality.

rows.recommendation: 3. In adults with COA, blood pressure measurement at rest in the upper and lower extremities is recommended as part of routine clinical assessment to screen for hypertension and residual/recurrent COA.
4. In adults with COA, ambulatory blood pressure measurement is reasonable to diagnose hypertension and monitor response to antihypertensive therapy.
5. In adults with COA, exercise testing is reasonable to screen for exercise-induced hypertension.
6. In adults with COA who present with exertional symptoms, evaluation for coronary artery disease is reasonable to guide management.
7. In adults with COA, screening for intracranial aneurysms by brain MR or CT angiography may be considered to guide management.

8. In adults with native or repaired COA, surgical or transcatheter stent therapy is recommended for anatomically and hemodynamically significant COA to prevent irreversible LV dysfunction from chronic pressure overload.
9. In adults with native or repaired COA and hypertension without hemodynamically significant COA, GDMT for hypertension is recommended to maintain controlled resting and ambulatory blood pressure.

content.title: 4.3.1. Ebstein Anomaly
content.narrative_summary: Synopsis describes Ebstein anomaly as an uncommon congenital heart defect occurring in about 1 in 1,000 live births. Although classically considered a malformation of the tricuspid valve, contemporary understanding recognizes an inherent RV cardiomyopathy that may extend to the left ventricle. The anomaly can be associated with ASD, VSD, and pulmonary stenosis, and a patent foramen ovale may significantly impact physiology. Accessory pathways and arrhythmias are relatively common. Patient surveillance and management vary based on age, lesion severity, and associated abnormalities including heart failure. (Text ends mid-sentence.)

rows.recommendation: In adults with Ebstein anomaly, an electrophysiological study is recommended for patients with symptomatic arrhythmia or asymptomatic ventricular preexcitation to assess for substrates for ablation, including multiple or high-risk accessory pathways.
In adults with Ebstein anomaly, CMR imaging can be useful to determine anatomy, RV dimensions, and systolic function to guide surgical planning and management.
In adults with Ebstein anomaly, electrophysiological study (and catheter ablation, if needed) can be useful before tricuspid valve surgery to improve clinical outcomes.

In adults with Ebstein anomaly, if transthoracic echocardiography is inadequate to guide surgical planning, transesophageal echocardiography can be beneficial to characterize tricuspid valve morphology and function.

In adults with Ebstein anomaly and severe RV dysfunction in whom there is concern that the RV will not support the entire stroke volume, preoperative diagnostic cardiac catheterization may be considered to assess candidacy for a bidirectional superior cavopulmonary (Glenn) anastomosis.

In adults with Ebstein anomaly and at least moderate tricuspid regurgitation in the presence of heart failure, worsening exercise capacity, or progressive RV systolic dysfunction, surgical intervention is recommended to restore valve function and augment cardiac output.
In adults with Ebstein anomaly and high-risk accessory pathway conduction or multiple accessory pathways, catheter ablation is recommended to reduce the risk for SCD.

In asymptomatic adults with Ebstein anomaly and at least moderate tricuspid regurgitation in the presence of progressive RV enlargement, systemic desaturation from a right-to-left atrial shunt, recurrent arrhythmias, and/or paradoxical embolism, surgical intervention can be beneficial to improve clinical outcomes.

In adults with Ebstein anomaly and severe RV dysfunction in whom there is concern that the RV will not tolerate supporting the entire stroke volume, a bidirectional superior cavopulmonary (Glenn) anastomosis at the time of tricuspid valve surgery may be considered in carefully selected individuals to improve cardiac output through ventricular unloading.

In adults with Ebstein anomaly who have an ASD/patent foramen ovale, and cyanosis or paradoxical embolism, isolated closure may be considered after hemodynamic assessment to improve clinical outcomes.

content.title: Valvular Pulmonary Stenosis
content.narrative_summary: Valvular pulmonary stenosis, a common congenital heart defect occurring in about 1 in 2,000 live births, is associated with a dilated main pulmonary artery and dysplastic valve cusps. Referral for intervention depends on obstruction severity, right ventricular pressure and function, and symptom presence. Mild native stenosis often has a benign course and may not require intervention. Severe stenosis typically requires intervention in childhood with good long-term prognosis. Moderate stenosis has more variable management, with some managed conservatively and others referred for catheter or surgical intervention. Outcomes after intervention relate to patient age, valve characteristics (morphology, diameter, gradient), and presence of genetic syndromes (eg, Noonan syndrome). Balloon valvuloplasty is a safe, effective first-line therapy and has largely supplanted surgical valvotomy.

rows.recommendation: In symptomatic adults with moderate or severe valvular pulmonary stenosis who have favorable valve anatomy, balloon valvuloplasty is recommended to improve symptoms.

In symptomatic adults with moderate or severe valvular pulmonary stenosis who are ineligible for or have had suboptimal results after balloon valvuloplasty, pulmonary valve replacement is recommended to improve symptoms.

In asymptomatic adults with moderate or severe valvular pulmonary stenosis and at least moderate tricuspid regurgitation or any RV dysfunction, pulmonary valve intervention is recommended to reduce pressure overload and improve valvular function.
In asymptomatic adults with severe valvular pulmonary stenosis, intervention is reasonable to reduce pressure overload and improve valvular function.

content.title: 4.3.5. Tetralogy of Fallot
content.narrative_summary: This page presents recommendations for adults with repaired tetralogy of Fallot (TOF), organized into diagnostic and therapeutic categories, with each recommendation assigned a Class of Recommendation (COR) and Level of Evidence (LOE). Referenced studies supporting these recommendations are summarized in the Evidence Table.

rows.recommendation: 1. In adults with repaired TOF, echocardiography is recommended for assessment of pulmonary and tricuspid valve dysfunction, right atrial size, ventricular size and function, residual VSDs, and estimation of RV systolic pressure to characterize residual hemodynamic sequelae.^1

2. In adults with repaired TOF and residual hemodynamic sequelae, CMR imaging is recommended for quantifying pulmonary valve function, ventricular size and function, and branch PA size and flow; characterizing the right and LVOT anatomy; quantifying residual shunts or aortopulmonary collateral flow; and assessing fibrosis of the ventricular myocardium.^2

3. In adults with repaired TOF undergoing right ventricle-to-pulmonary artery (RV-to-PA) conduit stenting or transcatheter pulmonary valve placement with a balloon-expandable platform, assessment of coronary artery compression risk is indicated to ensure absence of coronary artery compression from stent/valve placement.^3
4. In adults with repaired TOF and native RVOT anatomy being considered for transcatheter pulmonary valve replacement, cardiac CT is recommended to determine anatomic suitability.^4,5

content.narrative_summary: Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) is a common congenital heart condition requiring lifelong surveillance, with arrhythmias becoming more prevalent over time and sequelae including right ventricular outflow tract dysfunction and pulmonary valve disease. Initial surgical repair strategies and later interventions focus on preserving pulmonary valve function. Patients with TOF are at risk of right ventricular dilation, branch pulmonary artery stenosis, residual ventricular septal defects, tricuspid regurgitation, left ventricular dysfunction, and aortic root dilation. TOF is associated with sustained ventricular tachycardia and sudden cardiac death, with risk increasing in adulthood.

content.narrative_summary: Pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum (PA-IVS) is a rare congenital heart lesion characterized by membranous or muscular atresia of the RVOT, resulting in RV pressure overload and potential RV-dependent coronary circulation; adults with PA-IVS often follow diverse surgical pathways in childhood and have a high incidence of atrial arrhythmias. Restrictive RV physiology may be associated with ventricular fibrosis and RV-dependent coronary circulation. Overall survival is worse, with elevated rates of sudden cardiac death and heart failure, and right atrial dysfunction correlates with clinical outcomes. Management recommendations for heart failure and transplantation are provided in Sections 3.6 and 4.4.5, and follow-up frequency depends on repair type, residual physiology, arrhythmia status, and comorbid cardiac disease.

content.narrative_summary: Double-outlet right ventricle is defined as both great arteries arising from the morphologic right ventricle, with variants approximating TOF or d-TGA. Initial surgical repair strategies include creation of a left ventricle-to-aorta intracardiac baffle through the VSD, RV-to-PA conduit placement, or Rastelli-type repair, depending on the anatomy. Complex variants (atrial isomerism, AVSD, multiple VSDs, hypoplastic ventricles, straddling AV valves, and PA anomalies) further influence the choice between biventricular and univentricular repair. LVOT obstruction may occur, warranting a team-based reevaluation of risk and need for reoperation, including routine assessment of patch integrity. content.narrative_summary: The Fontan procedure allows systemic venous blood to flow to the pulmonary arteries in the absence of a subpulmonic ventricle and is used to palliate single-ventricle congenital heart disease. It is defined by obligate systemic venous hypertension and low cardiac output, and long-term exposure leads to multisystem disease and circulatory failure. Management of adults with Fontan circulation focuses on identifying and treating lesions or physiologic states that accelerate circulatory failure in a multidisciplinary setting, with routine evaluation and surveillance of affected organs—especially the liver—with referral to hepatology and other subspecialists as needed. Medical therapies are limited primarily to thromboprophylaxis, and arrhythmia management and structured exercise programs may offer benefit.

rows.recommendation: The decision to proceed with heart transplantation in adults with Fontan circulation is complex. Careful assessment of each patient’s anatomy and physiological state is necessary to balance the procedural and perioperative risks with potential benefits. Although cardiac transplantation can be performed successfully in adults with Fontan circulation, careful planning by a diverse multidisciplinary team with experience in Fontan transplantation is necessary to address pretransplant optimization, intraoperative planning, and postoperative care. Teams should have representation across specialties, including ACHD, heart failure/transplantation, congenital heart disease surgery, transplant surgery, cardiac anesthesia/critical care, cardiac imaging, hepatology, social work, and psychiatry. Additional subspecialty representation may be required, depending on the unique needs of the patient. The role for combined heart-liver transplantation in adults with Fontan circulation remains uncertain. Some studies have suggested improved outcomes in patients with evidence of liver cirrhosis and clinical evidence of portal hypertension, including ascites, varices, and splenomegaly, but prospective studies and long-term data are lacking. Those studies are limited by a small number of adults with Fontan circulation undergoing recent heart-only transplantation who have similar degrees of FALD, compared with combined heart-liver transplantation recipients, and by a paucity of studies on the trajectory of FALD after heart-only transplantation in adults. Published experiences of patients undergoing combined heart-liver transplant in adults with Fontan circulation show similar survival rates as in heart-only transplantation recipients but high rates of postoperative complications and lengthy posttransplant hospitalizations. Patients with decompensated FALD—manifesting as cirrhosis on pathology with clinical evidence of portal hypertension including variceal disease, ascites, and splenomegaly—benefit from evaluation by transplant hepatology at the time of referral for heart transplantation. The complex decision to proceed with combined heart-liver transplantation should be made for each patient by a multidisciplinary team with expertise in performing combined heart-liver transplantation in adults with Fontan circulation and who have extensive knowledge of locally available expertise.

In adults with Fontan circulation and high-grade atrioventricular block, epicardial apical site pacing may be associated with greater ventricular synchrony and a lower rate of ventricular dysfunction. Determination of the appropriate pacing strategy in adults with Fontan circulation and atrioventricular block should be made by an electrophysiologist with experience in device therapy.

Exercise training in adults with Fontan circulation has low risk and has shown benefits that include improvements in peak VO2 and quality of life across different exercise modalities. Because many adults with Fontan circulation may be prone to a sedentary lifestyle and have a predisposition to reduced skeletal muscle mass and increased adiposity from perceived limitations and prior instructions to minimize physical activity, clinician-directed, supervised exercise programs may offer particular benefit. Resistance training, particularly of the lower extremities, may offer advantages in this population by facilitating increases in muscle mass and venous return.

Catheter ablation can substantially reduce atrial arrhythmia burden in adults with Fontan circulation. Scar-mediated intra-atrial reentrant tachycardia and focal atrial tachycardias predominate, and treatment frequently requires integration of multiple interventions, including anticoagulation, cardioversion, antiarrhythmic medical therapy, pacing, and catheter ablation. Management should be performed in consultation with ACHD providers and electrophysiologists with experience in managing adults with Fontan circulation. Because catheter ablation of atrial arrhythmias in this population is associated with significant challenges, including multiple arrhythmia circuits, difficult access, atrial scarring, and a high risk for conduction system injury, it should be performed only by electrophysiologists with expertise in ablation of patients with Fontan circulation.

content.narrative_summary: Eisenmenger syndrome results from intra- and/or extracardiac left-to-right shunt defects leading to high pulmonary vascular resistance and subsequent bidirectional shunting. Risk of syndrome development is influenced by congenital syndromes, cardiac anatomy, shunt size, genetic and environmental factors. Chronic cyanosis, abnormal loading, and perfusion abnormalities contribute to multi-organ dysfunction, arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death. Patients with Eisenmenger syndrome, particularly those with Down syndrome, have lower exercise tolerance, more comorbidities, and standard risk tools (e.g., 6-minute walk) are less accurate. Supplemental oxygen should be individualized; high-altitude, pregnancy, extreme environments, nephrotoxin exposure, extreme exertion, and large intravascular volume shifts should be avoided.

Point 5: Data on upfront combination pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) therapy versus monotherapy in adults with Eisenmenger syndrome are limited. One study comparing combined sildenafil and ambrisentan versus sildenafil alone showed improved 6-minute walk distance, New York Heart Association functional class, and lower pulmonary pressures in the combination group; addition of a second PAH therapy in deteriorating patients was associated with improved functional class, walk distance, oxygen saturation, NT-proBNP levels, and pulmonary vascular resistance, with minimal systemic vascular resistance reduction and increased Qp:Qs. Triple vasodilator therapy data are scarce, and inhaled iloprost and the oral analog selexipag are less conclusive. Intravenous prostacyclin is typically avoided.  
Point 6: Arrhythmias are a major cause of morbidity and mortality in adults with Eisenmenger syndrome due to hemodynamic and shunt instability; prompt cardioversion with expert anesthesia support is recommended, even in hemodynamically stable atrial arrhythmias.  
Point 7: Supervised mild-to-moderate intensity exercise appears safe. A retrospective study of 20 PAH patients (10 with Eisenmenger syndrome) showed that 3 weeks of in-hospital training plus 15 weeks home training improved 6-minute walk distance and oxygen consumption but not World Health Organization functional class. In a subgroup with congenital heart disease, home-based training improved 6-minute walk distance versus no training. Patients should avoid very strenuous activity, competitive sports, and extreme isometric exercise.  
Point 8: See Table 43 for PAH-directed medication trials in Eisenmenger syndrome. Inhaled prostacyclin improved hemodynamics, RV function, oxygenation, symptoms, and functional class in a small prospective adult study. Retrospective data on subcutaneous treprostinil show functional and hemodynamic benefits; inhaled iloprost showed no benefit. Oral prostacyclin analog selexipag has no proven clinical efficacy, and riociguat data are lacking. Prostacyclin therapy may be considered for symptomatic or escalating patients when oral therapies fail.  
Point 9: Thrombosis is common in Eisenmenger syndrome, related to dilated pulmonary arteries, dysfunctional chambers, arrhythmias, intracardiac prosthetic material, and pacemaker leads. Observational studies report up to 30% laminated thrombi and 8%–14% cerebrovascular events. Systemic anticoagulation’s timing, type, and efficacy are unknown, but may be reasonable for patients with prior thromboembolic episodes or pulmonary arterial thrombosis without major bleeding.
